Thank you for this insightful question. The omnidirectional and broadband capabilities of our sensor stem from two fundamental design principles that distinguish it from conventional optical ultrasound sensors.
a. Active laser cavity versus passive resonant cavity
The key distinction lies in how acoustic signals are amplified. Passive Fabry-Pérot cavity sensors use an external laser to interrogate a high-Q resonator. To achieve high sensitivity, they require high Q-factors (10⁶-10⁸), which necessitates precise wavelength locking between the external laser and cavity resonance. This approach faces an inherent trade-off between sensitivity and stability.
Our active fibre laser cavity takes a fundamentally different approach. The fibre itself is the laser source, and acoustic pressure directly modulates the lasing process. Stimulated emission continuously amplifies the acoustic-induced phase modulation without relying on ultra-high Q-factors. Additionally, the self-contained laser architecture eliminates the need for external laser sources and wavelength locking systems, significantly simplifying the system and improving operational stability—particularly important for in vivo applications where environmental fluctuations can disrupt passive cavity wavelength alignment.
A detailed response comparison is provided in Supplementary Note S5c and Figure S19, with a detailed description of the ultrasound detection mechanisms.
b. Omnidirectional detection through cylindrical symmetry
The fibre's cylindrical geometry (62.5 μm diameter) is inherently symmetric in all radial directions, meaning it responds equally to acoustic waves arriving from any angle in the transverse plane. This enables 180° angular coverage without requiring mechanical scanning or complex sensor arrays. The miniaturized dimension—comparable to the acoustic wavelength at tens of MHz—also minimizes spatial averaging effects that would otherwise degrade high-frequency sensitivity. In contrast, many optical sensors employ planar membrane structures optimized for acoustic waves arriving perpendicular to the surface, resulting in limited angular acceptance and directional sensitivity. Experimental validation of our sensor's omnidirectional response is shown in Supplementary Figure S3c-d.
We have added detailed sensor characterization (Supplementary Note S1b and Figure S2), frequency response analysis (Supplementary Note S1c and Figure S3), and comprehensive comparison with state-of-the-art optical ultrasound sensors (Supplementary Note S5b and Tables S1-S2) to further clarify these technical distinctions. We have also incorporated relevant details into the first part of the results in the main text.
2. The authors state that the sensing area of a single fibre-laser transducer is ~300 times smaller than that of conventional piezoelectric transducers. Under such conditions, how is the field of view not compromised in this system? What specific factors or design features compensate for the reduced sensing aperture and ensure sufficient coverage for wide-field imaging?
Response:
Thank you for this important question. The relationship between sensor size and field of view in our system may appear counterintuitive, but it reflects a fundamental principle of photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) [1, 2].
a. Field of view is determined by synthetic aperture
In PACT, the field of view is not limited by the physical sensing area of an individual transducer. Instead, it is determined by the synthetic aperture formed through scanning or array configuration. The imaging principle works as follows: the fibre sensor scans linearly across the sample, acquiring photoacoustic signals at multiple positions. For each acoustic source, signals detected at different sensor positions arrive with characteristic time delays determined by acoustic propagation distances. By coherently synthesizing these time-delayed signals through back-projection reconstruction, we recover the spatial distribution of acoustic sources. Therefore, the field of view in this synthetic aperture approach is determined by: (1) the scanning range, which defines the lateral coverage, and (2) the angular acceptance of each sensor, which determines the depth range that can be effectively imaged. (Supplementary Figure S5)
b. Smaller sensors enable larger angular acceptance
Critically, our miniaturized sensor provides a key advantage: smaller sensors offer wider angular acceptance. Spatial averaging effects scale with sensor dimensions—a sensor large compared to the acoustic wavelength exhibits directional sensitivity with narrow acceptance angle, whereas a sensor comparable to or smaller than the wavelength responds uniformly to acoustic waves from different directions. Our fibre sensor (62.5 μm cladding diameter, with 7 μm core diameter) is significantly smaller than the acoustic wavelength at the center frequency (~20 MHz, corresponding to ~75 μm in water), enabling near-omnidirectional detection with 180° angular coverage in the transverse plane (Supplementary Figure S3c-d). This wide angular acceptance translates to a large effective aperture for tomographic reconstruction, enabling a field of view of 10 × 10 mm²—significantly larger than the physical sensor dimension.
In contrast, conventional piezoelectric transducers with larger sensing areas (typically 0.5-2 mm diameter) exhibit limited angular acceptance, requiring more complex array configurations or mechanical scanning schemes to achieve comparable coverage. Our approach demonstrates that miniaturization, when combined with synthetic aperture imaging, actually enhances rather than compromises the field of view. Critically, artifacts exhibit characteristic morphological signatures (e.g., streaking, blurring) and lack physiological responsiveness to stimuli, whereas true vessels display coherent dynamic changes during functional challenges.
(2) Multi-modal validation: We performed parallel imaging of mouse brain vasculature using 9.4T MRI angiography as ground truth (Supplementary Figure S18). Quantitative comparison of representative vessels in the hippocampal region shows excellent agreement in diameter measurements, with matched branching patterns and anatomical distributions, confirming that high-frequency signals originate from genuine vascular structures.
(3) Physiological validation: For human skin microvasculature, we validated vascular authenticity through dynamic functional challenges—brachial artery occlusion induced progressive signal reduction followed by reactive hyperemia, thermal stimulation produced vasodilation, and exercise revealed increased perfusion—with all responses spatially localized to anatomically appropriate vessels and following expected temporal dynamics.
The spatial distribution of S factor values revealed distinct skin regions, including the palm, dorsal forearm, and fingertip, and effectively captured the decrease in oxygenation changes during arterial occlusion-reperfusion cycles. These experimental results are in agreement with existing reports and well-documented physiological phenomena. Additionally, we performed co-localized transcutaneous oxygen tension (TcPO₂) measurements using a clinical monitor (TCM4, Radiometer) to validate the physiological relevance of our S factor-based oxygenation mapping (Figure 5p). Importantly, reconstruction artifacts would not exhibit such coherent spatiotemporal patterns or correlate with independent physiological measurements. The rare-earth-doped active fibre enables the integration of the laser source and acoustic sensor into a single device by forming a laser resonant cavity within the fibre itself. This integrated design offers two key advantages: (1) it provides intrinsically low-noise laser emission, eliminating the need for external laser sources and associated coupling losses; and (2) it produces significantly larger phase shifts in response to acoustic perturbations due to the intracavity amplification effect, thereby enhancing acoustic sensing sensitivity. We added detailed descriptions in Supplementary Note S5c.
By precisely controlling the grating inscription depth, the fibre sensor operates as a single-polarization, single-longitudinal-mode laser. The emission spectrum is shown in Supplementary Note S1a and Figure S1b, with a center wavelength of ~1550 nm and FWHM of <0.1 nm, confirming stable single-mode operation essential for high-sensitivity heterodyne detection.

Response:
Thank you for this insightful question. The MOBILE system employs a linear fibre sensor for 2D imaging with integral projection within a ~3 mm-thick detection imaging plane, with negligible out-of-plane signal interference (Supplementary Note S2, Figure S5, and also the following two reference papers).
The system is optimized for high-speed 2D hemodynamic monitoring rather than 3D volumetric imaging.
For 3D imaging, strategies include rotational scanning with tomographic reconstruction, acoustic focusing elements, or curved fibre arrays for depth sectioning. These extensions maintain fibre-based detection advantages—high sensitivity, large angular coverage, and flexibility. We have addressed this in the Discussion and Conclusion section.
